examShortTricks: Trick 1: Desert adaptations: thick cuticle/succulence (cactus CAM photosynthesis — stomata open at night), long roots, reduced leaves (spines); animals: kangaroo rat uses metabolic water, nocturnal habits — pair plant + animal.
Trick 2: Aquatic adaptations: floating leaves (water lily broad, waxy), hollow stems (buoyancy), air bladders in fish, webbed feet — the hydrophyte set.
Trick 3: Altitude adaptation in humans: more RBCs, higher haemoglobin — the physiological response line.
Trick 4: Thermoregulation classes: eurythermal vs stenothermal; homeotherms vs poikilotherms — the four vocabulary terms earn the definition marks.
keyPoints: Adaptations are inherited features that improve survival in a habitat.
Desert plants show CAM photosynthesis and reduced leaves.
Aquatic plants have broad floating leaves and air spaces.
High-altitude dwellers compensate with more haemoglobin.
practiceQuestions: Q. How do desert plants photosynthesise while saving water? (2 marks) — CAM: stomata open at night, CO2 stored as organic acids for daytime use.
Q. What is a stenothermal organism? (1 mark) — one that tolerates only a narrow temperature range.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Growth equations: exponential dN/dt = rN (J-curve, unlimited); logistic dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K (S-curve, carrying capacity K) — quote both equations and their curve shapes.
Trick 2: r-strategists: small, short-lived, many offspring, unstable habitat; K-strategists: large, few offspring, stable habitat — the contrast pair.
Trick 3: Interactions table: mutualism (+/+), competition (−/−), predation (+/−), parasitism (+/−), commensalism (+/0), amensalism (−/0) — six signs, six marks.
Trick 4: Gause's principle: two species with identical niches cannot coexist — competitive exclusion; resource partitioning is the escape.
keyPoints: Exponential growth follows dN/dt = rN; logistic growth levels at carrying capacity.
Population growth is regulated by density-dependent and independent factors.
Species interactions range from mutualism to competition and predation.
Competitive exclusion: complete niche overlap cannot persist.
practiceQuestions: Q. Write the logistic growth equation and define K. (2 marks) — dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K; K = carrying capacity.
Q. What is competitive exclusion? (1 mark) — one species eliminates another when their niches fully overlap.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Structure = biotic (producers, consumers, decomposers) + abiotic (inorganic/organic substances, climate) — list both columns.
Trick 2: Productivity chain: GPP − R (respiration) = NPP; NPP is the energy available to consumers; units kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ — the GPP/NPP relation is the core numerical.
Trick 3: Decomposition steps: fragmentation → leaching → catabolism → humification → mineralisation — five steps in order; humus is dark, amorphous, slow-decomposing.
Trick 4: Pyramid of energy is ALWAYS upright (10% law); biomass/number pyramids can invert (ocean) — the exception line.
keyPoints: An ecosystem comprises biotic communities and abiotic factors.
NPP = GPP − respiration; it supports consumer levels.
Decomposition proceeds through fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification and mineralisation.
Energy flow follows the 10% law with an always-upright energy pyramid.
practiceQuestions: Q. Distinguish GPP and NPP. (2 marks) — GPP is total capture; NPP = GPP − respiration is what accumulates.
Q. Name the steps of decomposition in order. (2 marks) — fragmentation, leaching, catabolism, humification, mineralisation.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Definition: gradual, predictable change of species composition culminating in a climax community — 'directional and predictable' are the keywords.
Trick 2: Stages: pioneer → seral stages → climax; hydrarch (water → forest) vs xerarch (bare rock → forest) — both END in mesic climax, the convergence line.
Trick 3: Pioneers: lichens on rock (xerarch), phytoplankton in water (hydrarch) — the two starting species.
Trick 4: Succession increases: species diversity, biomass, NPP-to-biomass ratio changes, soil depth — the four trends.
keyPoints: Succession: orderly species replacement over time towards a climax.
Pioneer species start succession (lichens on rock, phytoplankton in water).
Hydrarch and xerarch succession both converge on a mesic climax.
Diversity and biomass rise during succession.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the pioneer species on bare rock. (1 mark) — lichens.
Q. What is a climax community? (1 mark) — the stable end community of succession in equilibrium with the climate.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Carbon: atmosphere ↔ photosynthesis/respiration; CO2 ~0.03–0.04% of air; largest reservoir = ocean; human addition = fossil fuels — the reservoirs in one line each.

Trick 2: Nitrogen: N2 (78% of air) unusable directly → fixation (Rhizobium, cyanobacteria, lightning) → nitrification (NH3 → NO2− → NO3−) → assimilation → denitrification (Pseudomonas back to N2) — the five stations.
Trick 3: Phosphorus: NO atmospheric phase — sedimentary cycle only; rock → soil → plants → animals → back by decomposers; slowest of the three.
Trick 4: Gaseous vs sedimentary: C and N are gaseous cycles (atmosphere reservoir), P is sedimentary (lithosphere) — the classification 2-marker.
keyPoints: Carbon cycles through photosynthesis, respiration and combustion.
Nitrogen requires fixation before organisms can use it.
The phosphorus cycle is sedimentary with no gaseous phase.
Decomposers return all three nutrients to the soil.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is the phosphorus cycle called sedimentary? (1 mark) — its main reservoir is rock/soil, not the atmosphere.
Q. Name the bacteria of nitrification and denitrification. (2 marks) — Nitrosomonas/Nitrobacter; Pseudomonas.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three pyramid types — number, biomass, energy; energy pyramid is ALWAYS upright (Lindeman 10% law); biomass inverted in the ocean (phytoplankton < fish standing crop at a moment); number inverted for a single tree's insects.
Trick 2: 10% law numerical: 10,000 J producers → 1,000 J herbivore → 100 J carnivore → 10 J top — one chain calculation earns the numerical mark.
Trick 3: Trophic level rule: an organism can occupy more than one level (human: primary + secondary consumer); only ~4–5 levels possible because energy dies out.
Trick 4: Standing crop = biomass at a given time; pyramids of biomass use standing crop — the definition line.
keyPoints: Ecological pyramids express number, biomass or energy per trophic level.
Energy pyramids are always upright due to the 10% law.
Biomass and number pyramids may invert in special cases.
Energy is lost as heat at every transfer; it never cycles.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is the pyramid of energy always upright? (2 marks) — energy is lost (heat, respiration) at each transfer, so higher levels hold less.
Q. Give an example of an inverted pyramid of biomass. (1 mark) — a marine ecosystem where fish biomass exceeds phytoplankton standing crop.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Three levels with examples: genetic (rice varieties, 50,000+ strains), species (India: ~45,000 plants, 90,000+ animals), ecosystem (forests, wetlands, coral reefs) — one example each.
Trick 2: Latitudinal gradient: species richness ↑ toward the tropics — three hypotheses: speciation time (stable climate), productivity, niche specialisation.
Trick 3: Species–area relation: log S = log C + Z log A; Z ≈ 0.1–0.2 mainland, 0.3–1.5 islands — the equation is the standard 2-marker.
Trick 4: India's status: mega-diverse country, 3 of 34 biodiversity hotspots (Western Ghats, Eastern Himalaya, Indo-Burma).
keyPoints: Biodiversity spans genetic, species and ecosystem diversity.
Species richness peaks in the tropics.
Species–area relationship: log S = log C + Z log A.
India is a mega-diverse nation with several biodiversity hotspots.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the three levels of biodiversity. (1 mark) — genetic, species, ecosystem.
Q. Write the species–area relationship. (2 marks) — log S = log C + Z log A.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: The 'evil quartet': habitat loss/fragmentation, over-exploitation, alien species invasion, co-extinctions — four causes, four marks.
Trick 2: Alien species examples: Lantana, water hyacinth (Eichhornia), Parthenium, Nile perch in Lake Victoria — quote two.
Trick 3: Consequences: ecosystem collapse, loss of ecosystem services (productivity, pollination, climate), ethical/aesthetic loss — the three-value framing.
Trick 4: Conservation split: in situ (biosphere reserves, national parks, sanctuaries — cheapest, evolution continues) vs ex situ (zoos, seed banks, tissue culture) — the standard 3-marker.
keyPoints: Major causes of biodiversity loss: habitat destruction, over-exploitation, invasive species, co-extinction.
Invasive aliens outcompete natives (Lantana, water hyacinth).
In situ conservation protects species in their habitat.
Ex situ conservation uses zoos, seed banks and tissue culture.
practiceQuestions: Q. Name the four main causes of biodiversity loss. (2 marks) — the evil quartet.
Q. Distinguish in situ and ex situ conservation. (2 marks) — on-site (national parks) vs off-site (zoos, seed banks).

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Pollutant table: CO (haemoglobin affinity → death), SO2/NOx (acid rain), particulates (respiratory disease), CFCs (ozone), lead (nervous system) — one effect each.
Trick 2: Acid rain chemistry: SO2 + OH → H2SO4; NOx → HNO3, pH < 5.6 — the two acid names earn the mark.
Trick 3: Control devices: electrostatic precipitator (99% particulates), scrubber (SO2 with lime spray), catalytic converter (CO/NOx/unburnt HC) — three devices, three mechanisms.
Trick 4: Delhi-style vehicle control: Bharat/CNG norms, catalytic converters, lead-free petrol — the policy line.
keyPoints: Major air pollutants: CO, SO2, NOx, particulates, CFCs.
SO2 and NOx form acid rain damaging forests and buildings.
Electrostatic precipitators and scrubbers clean industrial emissions.
Catalytic converters reduce vehicle emissions.
practiceQuestions: Q. Why is CO lethal? (1 mark) — it binds haemoglobin ~200× more strongly than oxygen, causing tissue anoxia.
Q. How does an electrostatic precipitator work? (2 marks) — charged particles are attracted to collector plates of opposite charge.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Eutrophication chain: nutrient (N, P) enrichment → algal bloom → O2 depletion → fish death → anaerobic decay (foul smell) — the five-step causal chain is the answer.
Trick 2: BOD: oxygen needed by microbes to decompose organic matter — higher BOD = more pollution; clean water BOD < 5 ppm; sewage treatment uses BOD reduction as its goal.
Trick 3: Biomagnification: DDT 0.003 ppb water → 25 ppm fish-eating birds (10 million×) — the classic magnification numerical; also mercury (Minamata).
Trick 4: Sewage treatment: primary (physical, settling) → secondary (biological, activated sludge) → tertiary (chemical); Flocs = masses of bacteria in aeration tanks.
keyPoints: Water pollution sources: sewage, industrial effluents, agricultural runoff.
Eutrophication depletes dissolved oxygen and kills aquatic life.
BOD measures biodegradable organic pollution.
Toxicants biomagnify up the food chain (DDT, mercury).
practiceQuestions: Q. What does high BOD indicate? (1 mark) — heavy organic pollution (more oxygen demanded by decomposers).
Q. Explain biomagnification with an example. (2 marks) — DDT concentrates ~10-million-fold from water to top predators.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Radiation types: alpha (stopped by skin/paper), beta (penetrates skin), gamma (deep penetration, most dangerous) — the penetration ladder.
Trick 2: Effects: somatic (cancer, burns, leukaemia in the exposed person) vs genetic (mutations in offspring) — the two-class division.
Trick 3: Case studies: Chernobyl (1986), Fukushima (2011), Hiroshima/Nagasaki — quote one with its lesson.
Trick 4: Radioactive waste disposal: shielded storage, deep burial, vitrification — the three strategies; half-life governs storage time.
keyPoints: Nuclear radiation damages cells by ionisation.
Gamma radiation penetrates deepest and is most hazardous.
Effects are somatic (cancer) and genetic (mutations).
Radioactive waste requires long-term shielded storage.
practiceQuestions: Q. Which radiation is most penetrating? (1 mark) — gamma rays.
Q. Distinguish somatic and genetic effects of radiation. (2 marks) — body cells of the exposed person vs germ cells affecting descendants.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Mechanism: greenhouse gases (CO2, CH4, N2O, CFCs) transmit incoming short-wave sunlight but absorb outgoing long-wave infrared → warming — the one-way valve picture.
Trick 2: Gas potency: CH4 ~25× CO2 (20-yr), CFCs thousands× — quote one multiplier; CO2 dominates by volume.
Trick 3: Consequences: sea-level rise (thermal expansion + ice melt), extreme weather, coral bleaching, disease spread — four consequences.
Trick 4: Controls: Kyoto Protocol/Paris Agreement, afforestation, renewable energy, energy efficiency — the policy plus practice list.
keyPoints: Greenhouse gases trap outgoing infrared radiation, warming the planet.
CO2, CH4, N2O and CFCs are the main greenhouse gases.
Global warming raises sea level and disrupts climate patterns.
Mitigation: cut emissions, expand forests, shift to renewables.
practiceQuestions: Q. How does the greenhouse effect work? (2 marks) — gases let sunlight in but absorb outgoing infrared, retaining heat.
Q. Name two greenhouse gases more potent than CO2. (1 mark) — methane and CFCs.
